Normalised hypergraph Laplacian

Source: R/hypergraph_laplacian.R
hypergraph_laplacian.Rd

hypergraph_laplacian() computes the normalised Laplacian of a hypergraph and returns it as a symmetric node-by-node matrix, the operator that hypergraph_cluster() and hypergraph_transduction() are built on. It comes in two forms. type = "zhou" is the Laplacian of Zhou, Huang and Schölkopf (2006), computed on the binary incidence pattern, so the values in the incidence cells play no part. type = "random_walk" is the Laplacian of Hayashi et al. (2020) for a random walk with edge-dependent vertex weights: the weighted incidence cells (for example the summed weights bipartite_groups() produces with weight) set where a walker that enters a hyperedge lands, and the walk, which is not reversible, is symmetrised through its stationary distribution (Chung 2005).

Both Laplacians are symmetric positive semi-definite with eigenvalues in [0, 2]. On a binary incidence with unit hyperedge weights the two forms coincide. The hypergraph must be connected, so the eigenvalue 0 occurs once; further eigenvalues close to 0 indicate groups of nodes that the walk seldom leaves, which is what hypergraph_cluster() partitions by.

Usage

hypergraph_laplacian(hg, type = c("zhou", "random_walk"), edge_weights = NULL)

Arguments

hg

The hypergraph: a net_hypergraph from build_hypergraph() or bipartite_groups(), with at least two nodes and one hyperedge. A hypergraph that is not connected has no unique stationary distribution and raises an error of class nestimate_hypergraph_disconnected; analyse its components separately.

type

The Laplacian. "zhou" (default) is the Zhou et al. (2006) Laplacian on the binary incidence pattern; "random_walk" is the Hayashi et al. (2020) random-walk Laplacian on the weighted incidence.

edge_weights

Positive hyperedge weights, one per hyperedge in the order of the incidence columns. Default NULL, which gives unit weights for "zhou" and, for "random_walk", the heuristic of Hayashi et al.: the population standard deviation of each hyperedge's non-zero incidence cells plus one, which is 1 on a binary incidence. A vector of the wrong length, or with a value that is not finite and positive, raises an error.

Value

A symmetric numeric matrix with one row and one column per node (the node names as dimnames). Its attributes record the type, pi (the stationary distribution of the walk, named by node) and edge_weights (the hyperedge weights used).

Details

For "zhou", with \(H\) the binary incidence, \(W\) the diagonal of hyperedge weights, \(D_e\) the hyperedge sizes and \(D_v\) the node degrees (the summed weights of the hyperedges a node belongs to), $$L = I - D_v^{-1/2} H W D_e^{-1} H^T D_v^{-1/2},$$ and the stationary distribution is proportional to \(D_v\). For "random_walk", a walker at node \(v\) picks a hyperedge containing it with probability proportional to its weight, then a node \(u\) of that hyperedge with probability proportional to the incidence cell \(\gamma_e(u)\). The stationary distribution \(\pi\) is the leading left eigenvector of this transition matrix \(P\), and \(L = I - (\Pi^{1/2} P \Pi^{-1/2} + \Pi^{-1/2} P^T \Pi^{1/2}) / 2\). The random-walk Laplacian, its stationary distribution and its default hyperedge weights follow the reference implementation in HyperNetX (laplacians_clustering.py).

References

Zhou, D., Huang, J., & Schölkopf, B. (2006). Learning with hypergraphs: Clustering, classification, and embedding. NeurIPS 19.

Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random walks, Laplacians, and clustering. CIKM 2020, 495-504. doi:10.1145/3340531.3412034

Chung, F. (2005). Laplacians and the Cheeger inequality for directed graphs. Annals of Combinatorics, 9(1), 1-19.

Examples

events <- data.frame(
  person = c("a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "d", "c", "d", "e", "e", "a"),
  meeting = c("m1", "m1", "m1", "m2", "m2", "m2", "m3", "m3", "m3",
              "m4", "m4"),
  hours = c(2, 1, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 2, 4, 1, 1)
)
hg <- bipartite_groups(events, player = "person", group = "meeting",
                       weight = "hours")
L <- hypergraph_laplacian(hg, type = "random_walk")
range(eigen(L, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values)
#> [1] -1.803454e-16  1.001279e+00
